A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ControlHair research, with matching methods, equations and principal experiments. Text, tables and figures are readable throughout. v3 includes Appendices A-D; v1 ends with references and has no separate appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative comparisons against Wan 2.1 and UniAnimate-DiT in Table 2, qualitative experiments, application demonstrations and an error-correction case study.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds measured pipeline runtimes, training-data composition statistics and supplementary generalization and failure examples.

M1.justification: The DiffLocks/Blender simulation, strand-map and pose controls, conditional diffusion architecture and LoRA training procedure remain unchanged. Section 4.2 newly explains why estimated strand maps are used instead of analytical maps, but documents the existing procedure rather than introducing a component.

E1.justification: v3 adds limited qualitative coverage of full-body and anime-style rapid-motion inputs using reconstruction controls (Appendix C), and kinky-hair and accessory cases (Appendix D). Section 6 also reports extreme wind/motion tests. The 10K training corpus, principal reconstruction task and three applications are retained.

E2.justification: Wan 2.1 and UniAnimate-DiT remain the evaluated comparators in Figure 5 and Table 2. Newly discussed methods such as PhysAnimator, HHAvatar, DGH and HAAR are not added to the experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: New analyses introduce manual annotation of 100 randomly sampled training videos and per-stage runtime measurement for an 81-frame video. Section 5.3 revises the baseline prompt description from VEO 2 prompts with motion annotations to manually annotated prompts, without establishing a rerun. The main test size, image metrics, training budget and output resolution remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands diagnostic analysis through a training-data composition audit, runtime bottleneck analysis, full-body/anime generalization checks and concrete reconstruction-error propagation cases. These address questions largely unexamined in v1. The existing error-correction example is retained as Figure 11, previously Figure 9; no component ablation is introduced.

E5.justification: v1's cinemagraph discussion mentions multiple generations as a way to obtain the desired static-human result; v3 removes this informal repeat-sampling disclosure. Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, confidence intervals, dispersion or significance tests, and no actual change in experimental run counts is established.

E6.justification: All Table 2 scores and rankings are unchanged, including ControlHair's 17.15 PSNR, 0.668 SSIM and 0.370 LPIPS. Added results include stage runtimes of 22, 326, 21 and 853 seconds, totaling 1222 seconds, sampled-dataset composition percentages, and supplementary generalization/failure findings. These extend characterization without demonstrating a comparative performance improvement.

T1.justification: Equations 1-7 retain the same problem formulation, simulation mapping, projection, control fusion and generation definitions. Neither version contains additional theorems or proofs; the new strand-map rationale is explanatory rather than a mathematical revision.

C1.justification: v3 removes the broad first-physics-informed-framework assertion from the abstract and narrows the introductory novelty claim to hair-related physics control. It explicitly targets portrait and digital-human hair rendering. The central pipeline contribution, baseline-superiority claim and three application claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and limitations: offline runtime, simulator divergence, motion blur, kinky-hair/accessory failures, and moderate versus severe upstream errors. It explains estimator consistency and qualifies generalization scope. Conversely, it removes v1's residual-human-motion caveats for bullet-time and cinemagraphs, and invokes video-derived reconstruction results when discussing simulator accuracy.

D1.justification: v3 adds inference hardware and stage timings, and documents selecting 10 reconstruction-test clips from about 100 candidates. The project-page address changes, while v1's planned code/model-release statement and square-cropping disclosure for hair try-on disappear. The PDFs do not establish newly released resources or changed training implementation.

R1.justification: v3 acknowledges PhysAnimator and distinguishes its 2D deformation setting, adds positioning against HHAvatar, DGH and HAAR, and cites Houdini as a possible simulator. References to Seedance, Pika and Open-Sora Plan disappear. These refine prior-work coverage and narrow novelty without replacing the central research positioning.

P1.justification: The title changes, the two video-diffusion related-work subsections are consolidated, and passages throughout the introduction, method and applications are condensed or clarified. Discussion is reorganized around supplementary analyses. The main section sequence and much of the original exposition remain.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, with widespread figure resizing and relocation. Table 1 is reorganized horizontally, Figures 3 and 4 are placed together and their illustrations are edited. New Figures 9 and 10 present generalization and failure cases; the original Figure 9 moves to the appendix as Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v3 improves transparency through measured inference costs, sampled training-data characterization, concrete failure examples and more carefully scoped novelty. These gains help readers assess the unchanged system, but the main 10-video comparison is unchanged and added generalization evidence remains qualitative. Removing static-human caveats and invoking reconstruction results as evidence about simulator accuracy temper the improvement.
